title: Anxiety's Body
hook: Anxiety is the body preparing for a danger that has not arrived, and from outside it is easily mistaken for rudeness, coldness or guilt.
why:
Anxiety is one of the most common experiences people have and one of the most misread. The new colleague who will not meet your eyes and answers in single words looks arrogant. The man at the party who stays by the wall gripping his drink looks unfriendly. The witness who fidgets and stumbles looks guilty. Each may be doing nothing more than coping with a body that is braced for a danger that is not there.

This chapter teaches what anxiety does to the body, how it shows from outside, why the things people do to manage it can make it worse, and how easily it is mistaken for something else. It also covers panic attacks, which are far more common than most people realise, and what to do when someone near you is having one. As in every chapter of this part, the aim is recognition and a kind response. Anxiety in its ordinary forms is part of being human; when it takes over someone's life, the right response is to help them reach treatment that works, not to diagnose it yourself.

teach.h: Anxiety is the alarm before the danger.
teach.p:
Psychologists often distinguish fear from anxiety. Fear is the response to a danger that is present: the car swerving towards you, the dog that lunges. Anxiety is the response to a danger that might come: the meeting tomorrow, the test results next week, the conversation that could go badly. The body's machinery is largely the same, the stress response described in the first chapter of this part, but in anxiety it runs ahead of events, sometimes for hours or days.

In small doses, anxiety is useful. It makes people prepare, check and take care. It becomes a problem when it is out of proportion to the real risk, when it lasts long after the risk has passed, or when it starts to shape a person's life around avoiding what they fear. Many people have an anxious temperament without ever having an anxiety disorder, and many people with severe anxiety hide it well.

For a reader, this has a clear consequence. When you see the signs of anxiety, you are seeing a body preparing for something. You do not know what, you do not know how serious it is, and you cannot tell from outside whether it is a passing worry, an anxious temperament or something that is taking over the person's life.

What you can usually tell is that the person's attention is partly elsewhere, on the danger they are anticipating, and that they are working harder than they appear to be just to be in the room with you.

An anxious person is often doing two things at once: talking to you, and watching for a threat you cannot see.
teach.disconfirm: If anxious people's bodies behaved no differently from calm people's, apart from what they reported feeling, anxiety would be invisible to a reader. The stress physiology described in this part makes that unlikely, though some people hide its outward signs very well.
teach.pullQuote: An anxious person is often doing two things at once: talking to you, and watching for a threat you cannot see.

teach.h: What anxiety looks like from outside.
teach.p:
Anxiety shows in most of the channels this book has described. The body tends to fidget: a knee bouncing, fingers tapping, a ring twisted, a pen clicked. Pacifiers increase, as the chapter on leakage and pacifiers described: hands to the neck, the face, the arms. Breathing quickens and rises, as the chapter on breath described, and the person may swallow often because the mouth goes dry. The voice tightens and may speed up or catch.

Gaze often changes. Some anxious people scan the room repeatedly, checking exits and faces. Many avoid eye contact, especially socially anxious people, for whom being looked at is the threat. Startle may be quicker: a dropped plate or a door slamming produces a bigger jump than it would in a calm person.

Some people go the other way. Instead of fidgeting, they freeze: very still, very quiet, answering in single words. Others become talkative, filling every silence to avoid the gaps where something might go wrong. Others become irritable, as the chapter on the I'm Fine mask described, which many men find easier to show than worry.

Anxiety also shows in behaviour over time: over-preparing, checking things several times, seeking reassurance, arriving very early, leaving very early, avoiding certain places or people.

None of these is specific to anxiety. Fidgeting can be boredom or ADHD; avoiding eye contact can be autism or culture; quietness can be introversion. As always, look for a change from baseline, a cluster, and a situation that might explain it.
teach.disconfirm: If fidgeting, gaze avoidance and quickened breathing were no more common in anxious moments than in calm ones, against a person's own baseline, they would tell you nothing about anxiety. Most people can observe the difference in themselves before a feared event.

teach.h: Safety behaviours keep the fear alive.
teach.p:
In 1995 David Clark and Adrian Wells described a model of social anxiety that has shaped its treatment ever since. A central idea is the safety behaviour: something an anxious person does in a feared situation to prevent the catastrophe they fear. Someone afraid of saying something stupid rehearses every sentence in their head before speaking. Someone afraid of being looked at avoids eye contact and stays at the edge of the room. Someone afraid their hands will shake grips a glass tightly or keeps them in their pockets.

The same year, Wells, Clark and colleagues described why these behaviours are a trap. They feel protective, but they stop the person from ever discovering that the feared catastrophe would not have happened anyway. The person leaves the party thinking *I got through it because I kept quiet*, not *people were friendly and nothing bad happened*. The fear survives intact for next time. Later treatment studies found that helping people drop their safety behaviours, while facing the situation, made treatment more effective.

Safety behaviours also change how anxious people look to others. Rehearsing sentences makes a person seem distracted. Avoiding eye contact makes them seem cold or evasive. Standing at the edge of the room makes them seem aloof. The very behaviours meant to prevent a bad impression often create one.

For a reader, recognising safety behaviours is a powerful correction. The man who seems uninterested in you may be working very hard to seem all right. And for yourself, if you carry anxiety, noticing your own safety behaviours is often the first step towards testing whether your fear is right.
teach.disconfirm: If dropping safety behaviours made no difference to how anxious people felt in feared situations, or made them worse over time, the model would be wrong. Treatment research built on the model found that dropping them helped.

teach.p:
Put the previous blocks together and you can see why anxiety is so often misread. The signs that anxious people show, and the behaviours they use to manage their anxiety, overlap almost exactly with the signs people associate with rudeness, coldness, arrogance, disinterest and guilt.

A job candidate who avoids eye contact, gives short answers and fidgets may be read as evasive, when she is terrified of interviews. A new colleague who eats alone and says little in meetings may be read as stuck-up, when he is rehearsing every sentence and finding none safe to say. A man questioned about a missing item who goes red, stumbles and touches his neck may be read as guilty, when he is anxious about being disbelieved, the Othello error described in the chapter on deception. A date who barely speaks may be read as uninterested, when she is overwhelmed.

The cost of these misreadings falls on people who are already struggling. Anxious people are often aware that they are coming across badly, which makes them more anxious, which makes them come across worse.

The correction is simple to state and harder to practise: when someone seems cold, rude or evasive, put anxiety on your list of rivals, early. Then respond in a way that would help if it were anxiety, and would do no harm if it were not: a little more warmth, a little more structure, a little less pressure. If the person is anxious, they will usually ease. If they are simply rude, you have lost nothing.

Before you decide someone is cold, consider that they may be frightened.
teach.disconfirm: If people you had read as cold or rude turned out, when you got to know them, rarely to have been anxious, the correction in this block would be unnecessary. Many people can think of someone they misjudged this way.

teach.h: Panic attacks are common, frightening and survivable.
teach.p:
A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes, with strong bodily sensations: a pounding heart, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness, trembling, sweating, tingling, nausea, and often a terrifying sense that something catastrophic is happening, a heart attack, collapse, losing control or going mad. The chapter on breath described how over-breathing can feed the loop.

Panic attacks are far more common than most people think. In 2016 Peter de Jonge and colleagues analysed surveys of over 140,000 adults in twenty-five countries. About one adult in eight reported having had a panic attack at some point in their life. Most of them had had more than one. But only a small minority went on to meet the criteria for panic disorder, in which recurrent attacks and the fear of further attacks come to dominate a person's life.

From outside, a panic attack may look like a medical emergency, and sometimes people having one are taken to hospital for chest pain. It may also look like nothing much: some people have panic attacks quietly, sitting very still, gripping a chair, breathing hard, while those around them notice only that they have gone pale and silent.

For the person having one, the most important things to know are that panic attacks are not dangerous in themselves, that they pass, usually within minutes, and that they are very treatable. For the person beside them, the most important thing is the response in the next block.

A panic attack feels like dying. It is not, and it will pass.
teach.disconfirm: If panic attacks were rare, affecting only a tiny fraction of people, recognising them would matter less for most readers. The survey found about one adult in eight had experienced at least one, which makes it likely you will be near someone having one.

teach.h: Helping someone through a panic attack.
teach.p:
If someone near you seems to be having a panic attack, the first step is to check whether it might be something else. Ask whether they have chest pain, especially spreading to the arm or jaw, whether they have a heart or lung condition, asthma or diabetes, and whether this has happened before. If you are unsure, or if they do not improve, call the emergency services. Calling for a panic attack is a far smaller mistake than not calling for a heart attack.

If it does seem to be panic, stay with them. Move somewhere quieter if you can. Kneel or sit beside them rather than standing over them. Speak slowly and calmly, in short sentences: *I'm here. This is panic. It will pass. You're safe.*

Help them slow their breathing without making it a demand. Breathe slowly yourself where they can hear and see you, with a long breath out, and if they are open to it, invite them to breathe out with you. Paper bags are no longer recommended. Some people find it helps to focus on their senses: naming five things they can see, four they can hear, three they can touch, which draws attention away from the alarming sensations.

Avoid *calm down*, *it's all in your head* and *you're fine*. Each tells the person that their experience is wrong, which adds fear. Do not crowd them, and do not leave them alone unless they ask for space.

Afterwards, they may be exhausted, embarrassed or shaky. Be matter-of-fact and kind. If attacks keep happening, or they start avoiding places or activities because of them, encourage them to see a doctor. Talking therapies for panic and anxiety have good evidence and help most people.
teach.disconfirm: If staying calmly with someone, breathing slowly beside them and reassuring them it will pass made no difference to how quickly a panic attack subsided, the advice in this block would add nothing. Most people who have had panic attacks say that calm company helped.

teach.h: Give control and predictability, not endless reassurance.
teach.p:
Anxiety feeds on uncertainty and on the sense of having no control, which the first chapter of this part described in the research on stress. That points to what helps an anxious person day to day. Tell them what will happen and when. Send the agenda before the meeting. Say who will be at the dinner. Offer choices: where to sit, whether to speak first or last, whether to talk now or later. Predictability does not cure anxiety, but it removes some of what anxiety latches onto.

Reassurance is more complicated than it seems. When an anxious person asks *Are you sure it'll be all right?*, the natural response is *Yes, of course*. Clinicians who treat anxiety often find that repeated reassurance brings short relief and then the question comes back, sometimes within minutes, and that answering it over and over can help keep the worry going. A kinder response, after the first reassurance, is often to help the person make a plan, or to acknowledge the worry without arguing with it: *It sounds like this is really worrying you. What would help you feel ready?*

Gentle encouragement to face, not avoid, feared situations also helps, at a pace the person chooses. Avoidance shrinks a person's life and confirms the fear; small steps towards the feared thing, with support, are at the heart of most effective treatments.

And know when to suggest more. If anxiety is stopping someone from working, sleeping, travelling or seeing people, or if they are using drink to cope, encourage them to see a doctor. Effective help is widely available, and most people who get it improve.
teach.disconfirm: If repeated reassurance reliably reduced anxious people's worry for good, rather than briefly, the caution in this block would be unnecessary. Notice, the next time someone asks for reassurance repeatedly, how long the relief lasts.

poseGallery.doCaption: Wondering whether he is anxious, and making it a little easier.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading his avoided eyes and short answers as arrogance.
poseGallery.annotation: The signs of anxiety overlap almost exactly with those people read as rudeness or coldness. Put anxiety on your list of rivals early.

poseGallery.doCaption: Dropping one safety behaviour, and finding the fear was wrong.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Gripping a glass at the edge of the room, never testing the fear.
poseGallery.annotation: Safety behaviours feel protective but stop people discovering that what they fear would not happen. Dropping them, with support, helps.

poseGallery.doCaption: Kneeling beside him: 'I'm here. This will pass.'
poseGallery.annotation: Telling someone in a panic that they are fine tells them their experience is wrong. Calm company and slow breathing help more.

poseGallery.doCaption: Acknowledging the worry, and making a plan together.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reassuring him for the tenth time that it'll be fine.
poseGallery.annotation: Repeated reassurance brings short relief and can keep worry going. A plan gives some control back.

caseStudy:
Richard, fifty, leads a small finance team. His newest hire, Ollie, twenty-eight, is excellent on paper and quiet in person. In meetings he looks at the table, answers in a few words and never volunteers anything. He eats lunch alone at his desk. Two colleagues tell Richard they find Ollie stand-offish.

Richard watches more carefully. He notices that Ollie's knee bounces under the table in meetings, that he grips his pen tightly, and that his voice is tight and quick on the rare occasions he speaks. Before his first presentation to the department, Ollie arrives forty minutes early, and his hands shake as he sets up. None of it looks like arrogance. It looks like a man working very hard to get through each meeting.

Richard changes a few things without commenting on any of them. He sends agendas a day ahead, and tells Ollie in advance which item he will be asked about. He holds short one-to-ones before big meetings, so that Ollie can rehearse his points with one person rather than ten. He asks a warm, easy-going colleague to invite Ollie to the team's Thursday lunch.

After a month, in one of their one-to-ones, Ollie tells him that he has struggled with anxiety since university, that meetings are the hardest part of his job, and that the agendas have made a real difference. Richard thanks him for telling him, asks whether there is anything else that would help, and mentions the company's employee assistance programme. He does not tell anyone else.

In March Ollie presents to the department again. His hands still shake a little when he sets up. Afterwards, at lunch, he tells a joke.
observe: Notice one person this week who seems cold, rude or uninterested, and look for signs that they might instead be anxious.
Notice your own safety behaviours in a situation that makes you uneasy: what you do to prevent the thing you fear.
Notice how often someone asks for reassurance about the same worry, and how long the relief seems to last.

drills.name: Rivals for Rudeness
steps: Recall three people you have judged as cold, rude or arrogant on first meeting.
For each, write what they actually did, as behaviour.
Write how each behaviour could be explained by anxiety.
Note anything you later learned about any of them.
Write one thing you could do differently on a first meeting with someone who seems cold.

drills.name: Safety Behaviour Audit
steps: Choose a situation that makes you mildly anxious, such as a party, a phone call or speaking up in meetings.
List everything you do in that situation to prevent what you fear.
For each, write what you fear would happen without it.
Choose one behaviour to drop next time, in a low-stakes version of the situation.
Afterwards, write what actually happened.

drills.name: Panic Response Card
steps: Write down the questions you would ask to check for a physical emergency.
Write the emergency number where you live, and when you would call it.
Write three short, calm sentences you would say to someone having a panic attack.
Write the grounding exercise of naming things you can see, hear and touch.
Keep the card in your wallet or phone and read it once a month.

drills.name: Predictability Offer
steps: Think of someone who seems anxious in a situation you share, such as a meeting or a family event.
Identify one piece of information you could give them in advance.
Identify one choice you could offer them.
Offer both, without mentioning anxiety.
Note any difference in how they seem.

drills.name: Reassurance Swap
steps: Recall a time someone asked you repeatedly for reassurance about the same worry.
Write what you said each time.
Write an alternative response that acknowledges the worry without arguing with it.
Write a question that would help them make a plan.
Practise both aloud.

quiz.q: A new colleague avoids eye contact, gives short answers and eats lunch alone. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That he is arrogant and has decided he does not want to mix with you
That he is hiding something, and will be found out before long
That he may be anxious; make things a little easier and more predictable
That he has social anxiety disorder and should be told to get help
quiz.explain: These behaviours overlap closely with anxiety and safety behaviours. A little more warmth and structure helps if he is anxious and costs nothing if he is not. Diagnosing him, to his face or to others, is not your role.

quiz.q: In the World Mental Health Surveys analysed by de Jonge and colleagues, roughly what share of adults had ever had a panic attack?
options: About one in eight, most of whom had more than one
About one in a hundred, nearly all of them women
About half of all adults in every one of the countries
Almost nobody outside a small number of wealthy countries
quiz.explain: About one adult in eight reported at least one panic attack, and most had had several, but only a small minority developed panic disorder. You are likely to be near someone having one at some point.

quiz.q: According to the cognitive model of social anxiety, why do safety behaviours keep fear going?
options: They make the feared situation far more dangerous than it really is
They draw attention to the person, which then confirms the fear
They tire the person out so that they cannot cope with the situation itself
They stop the person discovering that the feared outcome would not happen
quiz.explain: Safety behaviours feel protective, but the person credits them with preventing a disaster that would not have happened. The fear survives intact, and dropping them, with support, helps treatment work.

quiz.q: A man in a café suddenly breathes very fast, grips the table and says he thinks he is dying. What fits this chapter?
options: Tell him firmly that it is only panic and that he will be absolutely fine in a minute
Check for chest pain or a known condition, stay calm beside him, breathe slowly
Give him a paper bag to breathe into until his breathing slows down again
Leave him to recover in peace, since crowding him will make it worse
quiz.explain: Check first for a physical emergency and call for help if unsure. If it is panic, calm company, slow breathing beside him and reassurance that it will pass help most. Paper bags are no longer advised.

quiz.q: Why can repeated reassurance backfire for an anxious person?
options: It makes the person angry with you for not taking them seriously
It tells the person that their worry is entirely justified and important
It brings short relief but can keep the worry coming back
It works so well that the person never learns to cope alone
quiz.explain: The relief fades and the question returns, sometimes within minutes. Acknowledging the worry and helping the person make a plan gives them some control, which tends to help more.

quiz.q: A friend has had several panic attacks this year and has started avoiding the supermarket where one happened. What fits this chapter?
options: Encourage him to see a doctor, since panic and anxiety respond well to treatment
Do his shopping for him from now on, so that he never has to go back there
Tell him to force himself to go every day until the fear goes away for good
Reassure him that panic attacks are harmless and that he should ignore them
quiz.explain: Recurrent attacks and growing avoidance are signs that help is worth seeking, and talking therapies have good evidence. Doing everything for him supports the avoidance; forcing him adds fear.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person you misjudged as cold, rude, uninterested or evasive, and later suspected might have been anxious, or think of a time you were misjudged that way yourself. Describe what the body and behaviour actually showed. What safety behaviours, if any, can you now see in it? What would have helped in the first few minutes? And what is one situation in your own life where you could drop a safety behaviour this month?
reflection.guidance: Many men recognise themselves in this chapter, sometimes for the first time. Describing your own safety behaviours precisely is useful: they are often small and habitual, such as rehearsing sentences or keeping hands in pockets. The last question is the practical one. Choose a low-stakes situation, so that you can find out whether the fear is right.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read anxiety as a character flaw, treating the anxious person as rude, cold, arrogant or guilty, and responding with coolness that makes them more anxious still. The second is the opposite: deciding that someone has an anxiety disorder and telling them or others so. The third is to respond to panic badly: telling someone to calm down, assuming panic when it may be a heart attack, or reaching for a paper bag. The fourth is to reassure endlessly, or to help someone avoid everything they fear, which keeps the anxiety going. And the most quiet failure is to miss your own anxiety and safety behaviours, which may be shaping your life more than you know. Warmth, structure, calm company, and encouragement towards treatment when it is needed, help most.
